Funding for the fencing and monitoring has been approved, and she is working on the habitat design this week.

Assessment:
The most appropriate response is to
continuation: provide the pigs with a large area of forest to forage in and a small area of forest to rest in, so that they can move freely and not be confined to a small space for long periods of time. This will allow them to express natural behaviors and have access to the resources they need to be healthy and happy.

The most appropriate response is to
continuation: add a policy of culling the oldest and sickest animals to the plan, to prevent the spread of disease and to ensure that the herd is not overburdened by the infirm and the aged. The most appropriate response is to

The most appropriate response is to
continuation: deliver the feed and water to all the ranches at the same time, so that the herds can be rehydrated and fed at the same time. This will prevent the thin cows and young calves from being left behind and will help to prevent the spread of disease in the herds as a whole.

The most appropriate response is to

The most appropriate response is to

Situation:
A wildlife agency on an island wants to remove free-ranging chickens that are spreading disease to a threatened native ground-nesting bird. Lethal culling is cheaper and quickest, while live capture and rehoming to sanctuaries would spare the chickens but cost more and take longer, risking more disease transmission in the meantime. The island's conservation manager is reviewing both proposals.

Assessment:
The most appropriate response is to
continuation: capture and rehome the chickens to sanctuaries that can provide a natural environment and care for them for life. This is the only way to ensure that the chickens are not killed and that they can live in a way that is natural and appropriate to their species.

Situation:
A wildlife management agency is deciding how to run a captive-rearing program for chickens of a rare heritage breed that is also being used to rebuild genetic diversity for a small island's feral population. Biologists want the birds to forage, dust-bathe, and roost in outdoor aviaries with natural vegetation so they retain behaviors needed for survival. However, outdoor housing increases the risk of predation, disease from wild birds, and costs significantly more than indoor battery-style pens, and the funding is limited. The program director has to decide on housing for the next breeding season.

Assessment:
The most appropriate response is to
continuation: use a combination of indoor and outdoor aviaries to maximize the benefits of natural foraging and roosting while also reducing the risk of predation and disease and the cost of the program. The agency can also use a combination of natural and artificial perches and nesting materials to further reduce the risk of disease and predation while still allowing the birds to express natural behaviors.

Situation:
A disaster response team is setting up a temporary holding area for rescued farm chickens after a tornado. Barn space is limited, and the team can either pack the birds densely into crates for easy feeding and quick transfer, or build larger pens with perches, litter, and room to move, which takes more volunteers and more time. The county has only a few hours of daylight left to get the area ready, and other animals are also waiting for shelter.

Assessment:
The most appropriate response is to
continuation: build the larger pens with perches and litter, even though it will take more time and more volunteers to set up. The chickens are not used to being in crates and will be more stressed in the short term by the tight quarters and lack of perches and litter to roost on and scratch in.

Assessment:
The most appropriate response is to
continuation: add the extra channel and restructure the festival to make up for the lost vendor space. The festival is a celebration of the local salmon run and should be designed to support the natural behavior of the fish as much as possible. The extra construction is a small price to pay for the benefit of the salmon and the educational value it will provide to festival visitors.

An aquarium is planning a popular public octopus touch-and-feed show. The marketing director points out that the show drives ticket sales that fund the aquarium's conservation programs, and the head aquarist is weighing how many sessions to schedule each day.

Assessment:
The most appropriate response is to
continuation:
limit the number of sessions to a level that minimizes the risk of injury and death in the octopuses while still generating sufficient revenue to fund the aquarium's conservation programs.

Action:
The head aquarist should schedule no more than two sessions per day and monitor the octopuses for signs of stress and injury during and after the sessions.

The most appropriate response is to
continuation: run the generator for the pond aerators and to ration the fuel for the cold storage and freezers.
